speechtext:
Yes, and I am still impatient to see it.
We are to come to grips with welfare, and to fight in a meaningful way for strengthening the position of women in our society and economy. In that respect I was very impressed by the Law Reform Commission under Mr. Justice Patrick Hart, which recently addressed itself to the problems of the family courts.
There is just one thing I would like to suggest here to the Law Reform Commission and to legislators. This refers to the deserted partner in an estranged marriage, usually a woman, and often a mother. Under existing circumstances an award is made by the court, and all too frequently the other partner, usually the husband, does not meet his payments. Frequently when the wife tries to chase him he moves to another jurisdiction, sometimes to another province, sometimes to another country, and she is left in a particularly vulnerable position. She has to hire lawyers and search her husband out, and because she has not received her payments she may have to go to work. Thereafter she may have to leave that work to pursue the legal procedures in relation to her missing payments.
All this is terribly unfair and I would urge that we, together with the provinces, acting in concert right across Canada-so that we do not get into jurisdictional disputes, and so that the deserted wife or mother does not suffer from such jurisdictional disputes-stipulate that when a court award is made it is to be paid by an arm of the
The Address-Mr. Danson
Crown, so that payment is assured to the mother, the wife, or to the husband, as the case may be. Then it would be up to the Crown to make certain that the husband acts, that he pays his alimony, that he pays the award made into a Crown fund. If he is delinquent the authorities would go after him and, if they cannot find him, then the fund would pay.
If the report of the Law Reform Commission is correct, welfare payments in this one area alone amount to $1 million a day. Such a fund, if established, would reduce these welfare payments substantially. I do not say that a scheme like this would reduce them completely, because usually alimony payments are not enough and it is necessary for further assistance to be provided. But the soul destroying experience that these women have to go through in this process is one that should not apply in our society today.

subtopic: THE PRICE OF CLOTHING WILL GO UP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE PRICE OF CLOTHING WILL GO UP
speechtext:
My wife told me to say that, Mr. Speaker. But it is something quite serious, and in a civilized and so-called advanced society we should not allow such a situation to exist when we can remedy it so easily. I urge this on the Law Reform Commission and on the ministers responsible for the legislation.
The Speech from the Throne goes on to mention improvements in the Canada Pension Plan in greater recognition of women's role in our society, and then goes into the whole question of science and technology. Mr. Speaker, all of these things may not appear to have very much to do with inflation itself, but they do help to make society more productive and thus, in my view, more competitive. As I see it, the only way we are really going to beat inflation is to produce, to be as productive as, or more productive than, our trading partners, to keep our productivity up and our costs down so that then we really will not have a problem with inflation.
The one matter that concerns most of us about the so-called oil crisis is the alternate uses of energy and the alternate sources of energy available to us. I am afraid that at least here in Canada we are becoming a little complacent about the oil shortage, because in effect we have got it made. This is one of our problems. We have got so much going for us, that all we need do is get used to living with the higher prices. Of course that is not nice, but we are able to adapt much more so than other countries.
We have other sources of energy that previously were not considered economic. The primary one in Canada is the Alberta tar sands. We knew these tar sands were there. We knew they were not economic to develop at existing world prices for oil, but regrettably they have now become economic for development.
While we have a short-term energy crisis we are aware, now more than ever before, that we have the ability to resolve it on a long-term basis and, I think, on a world scale. It requires only the will and the commitment of the resources to do so. The oil producing states have made us aware of the great opportunity Canada has to upgrade its economy with existing resources.

February 28, 1974
The Address-Mr. Danson
It is not generally realized that Canada possesses massive coal reserves, primarily in Alberta and British Columbia, which offer a further major energy source for us. The remoteness of these reserves from the major eastern industrial centres, the transportation costs, plus the access of western users to our oil and gas producing areas, have retarded the development of these coal reserves. The major exception is the coal being shipped in large volume to Japan. The coal which eastern Canadians do use is usually imported from the more accessible American coal fields in Pennsylvania and West Virginia. Certainly that applies in Ontario in respect to coal used by Ontario Hydro.
These coal reserves offer a major ace in the hole for Canada, and give western Canada still another resource on which it can build a significant industrial economy in the years to come. The coal, like western oil and gas, can be converted in the west, with its valuable by-products being shipped in a more sophisticated form to the rest of Canada and, when in long-term surplus, to the rest of the world, naturally at the higher prices that more refined processing brings with it.
This is one indication of how the current crisis has made us aware of the necessity to develop alternate energy sources. With coal, the supply and the technology are largely available to us. Other resources with equal or greater potential require new technology or further development of existing technology. Nuclear power is one of the most obvious, and even existing technology becomes more competitive with escalating oil prices. Canada has both the technology and the uranium reserves. I think we have been fortunate in "hanging tough" with the CANDU, which some people thought was a mistake. They thought we were on the wrong track with our heavy water process but it turns out that we seem to be right. Other countries are now looking at us with great respect and great interest.
There are other limitless renewable resources of energy. Solar energy potential is so great that the harnessing of only a miniscule amount dissipated daily can provide all the heat and power required for our needs. That is easy to say, but you have to harness it and store it.
The processing of human and animal waste is another source of an almost infinite nature. We thought this was sort of funny. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) has been saying it for some time. Pig farmers in England have been driving their cars on the methane gas produced from pig waste and from garbage. It is a serious source of energy. If any of you have heard of the explosion of buried garbage dumps, that is caused by the methane gas which is generated in the decaying process.

subtopic: THE PRICE OF CLOTHING WILL GO UP
speechtext:
I am not an expert but I am interested and I would like to become expert. I think we should all address ourselves to these problems because they are rather important.
The capturing of tidal power and conventional hydro-electic power of a non-depleting nature has ecological

impact which makes it imperative that we approach it only with very special care and sensitivity. There are some great experts like the Rothchilds. I always say they have water on the brain because they always see things in terms of water resources and power. Also we see some bad ecological effects from rather good programs, such as the Aswan Dam. We should be able to avoid these in the future.
The options are many but the task itself is massive. No one can say which is the best, the most economical, and the most environmentally desirable. One type may be best for Canada but not for other nations, and the reverse is also true. The developing nations' needs and technology may require different responses than those of the industrial nations.
Today I was at lunch at the home of the Indian High Commissioner and was interested to meet a young commercial attache who told me that in India, where they have a very serious energy problem-not the result of luxury as only 8 per cent of their gas goes into cars and trucks, some going to make simple things like kerosene which the ordinary person in India uses for cooking, the remainder being used for industrial processes-the additional cost of energy for them is of great importance. But it is something which they must face and which I think we must face.
I also learned that they have massive coal reserves in India. That is something I never knew. I did not know I was going to be speaking tonight-although I knew I was going to speak in this debate-and I was going to get the figures. With a population of some 500 million in India, they have reserves which, this young attache says, could last them hundreds and hundreds of years. In any event, they appear to be massive. So you can use technology for gasification. Sometimes these embassy parties are not all bad. An attache from the South African embassy told me that a high percentage of their oil and gas is produced from coal. It is higher cost. They import some, but they still produce a major portion of their requirements from coal. So the technology is available around the world, if we could just harness and refine it.
The whole task must be approached with the same urgency and allocation of intellectual and material resources that produced the first atomic bomb and the space programs in the United States and the U.S.S.R. It is a major, massive commitment of resources on a greater scale than we have seen in the past. In this case, fortunately, it is for peaceful purposes and for all mankind. I think it offers a unique opportunity for international co-operation and sharing that has not heretofore been realistically existent. No time should be lost, I suggest, and I think Canada can play a significant role. Indeed, I think we can take the initiative, take the lead and act as the catalyst for this program in the world today. It does not matter who gets the credit, though we are in a good position as we are well respected in this field internationally. We have an energetic energy minister who can take the ball and run with it so I think we could really do a great service to mankind.
The project must include all interested nations, and particularly those with a resource potential or scientific capability. All technological input must be pooled and the
February 28, 1974

results acceptable to everyone. Needs, resources and potential techniques should be defined and the tasks allocated. It might be sub-divided with designated nations, or groupings of nations, forming the nucleus for the specialized research efforts and taking the lead. For instance, Canada might be the centre for all the nuclear development or perhaps the heavy water development, or we might take the lead in coal processing. The United States could take the lead in solar energy, as that is a massive one. The common market might join forces in the field of animal and human waste. Eastern European nations, the socialist states, if they come into it-and I think they should-could co-ordinate coal processing. The Scandinavian countries could take on hydro-electric development, the Soviet Union could perhaps take on natural gas, and Japan could take on oil technology. I think we could learn a great deal from them.
None of these nations would have a monopoly, nor would they necessarily provide the greatest input in the area of their responsibility. They would provide the administrative, co-ordinating and publishing functions of the efforts of scientists and engineers in all participating nations. Teams would be operating throughout the world and the scientific cross-pollination could result in major break-throughs and immense spin-offs in developments which are quite unpredictable at this time. For example, a great deal of our computer technology is a result of the requirements of the space program. There are sophisticated metallurgical processes as a result of this program. There is transistor technology too. Do hon. members remember about five years ago when we used to have tubes in our radios? We do not see those any more because we have transistors. This is part of the scientific, technological and industrial fallout from all of these programs. We can see it in our own country in programs like the CF-100 or the STOL aircraft. There is technological fallout and skills which come as a result of these programs, and people are using them on a much more refined basis than ever before.
It is even conceivable that the United Nations, through a new agency and a secretary general for energy, could be the catalyst for something like this. I think it deserves that sort of priority. The important thing is to have the will, to get the ball rolling on a scale and with a degree of urgency that has never before been conceived, with the participation and co-operation of all nations. It is rarely that a world crisis can benefit all people and all of the nations on this earth by the harnessing of the natural and human resources which are the heritage of everybody on earth. I would urge consideration of this suggestion by this government, by this country and by the entire world.
There are other things in the throne speech which give food for thought. One was the greater utilization and more refined use of manpower. I have been concerned that some 50 per cent of our work force is under the age of 25. This is the result of the baby boom. I do not know why we did not see them coming. I think they still took nine months in those years, but somehow we did not calculate their arrival. We saw them coming through our public schools and our high schools, through our universities and into our work force, but we were surprised every time. Members of parliament will be standing in this place in the year 2005 or 2015 saying "Who are all these people who are getting
The Address-Mr. Danson
their old age pensions?" They will be products of the baby boom that we started in our passion.

speechtext:
Well, I have done pretty well and I have no complaints. This gives us the fastest growing labour force in the world, and this group will be with us, being absorbed into the work force, until 1980.
As a result of this there are many serious problems. Some of you may have read-certainly the people in the Toronto area will have,-about a 16 year old girl from Elliot Lake who hanged herself in a cell in Toronto's dirty old Don jail. Now you wonder what has happened to this girl (a) that she was put there, and (b) that she was so distraught that she hanged herself. You see the reaction of the judge, Judge Addison, a humane sort of person who is sick and sorry from what he sees has happened-not because of his fault-trying to allocate the blame, trying to be blamed. I could not help but wonder about her parents up in Elliot Lake. They had a little blond child-I do not know if she was blond-on their knees and I am sure there was a very proud father who wanted to see her through school and marriage and have grandchildren. Yet he probably saw her wracked with drugs through an over permissive society, and she just disappeared from the scene. She was a babysitter in Toronto and was accused of stealing Christmas gifts from the place where she was sitting. She had been in constant trouble. What sort of trauma affected this girl? What has happened to our society when we can let this sort of thing happen? I think this touched people in our area very deeply. On the surface, it appears that the girl stole some Christmas gifts. That was pretty mean. This was a 16 year old girl. What is happening in a society which can produce this sort of thing?
I suggest that we have not moved fast enough. I think we have done a great deal by introducing programs such as Opportunities for Youth, Local Initiatives, the Company of Young Canadians and other imaginative programs. We have let the kids do their own thing. Really, what they need desperately is some help in doing their own thing. I think some of the organized institutions in our society were pretty staid. They were not communicating with these kids. But they have learned and they have been shaken up. That is why certain agencies have become involved with our imaginative and bright youth in giving us great programs.
These kids grew up in a gentle and kind society which allowed them to do what they did. They had a secure base from which to work and they had time with which to work. I do not know if we are all the same, but when I was growing up you looked after yourself or you were not looked after. That was not so terrible. I was told that it was terrible. I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) the other day talking, on a program, about the depression. Some people said the depression was terrible; others thought it was fun. I did not even know we were poor. I just thought that is how things were.
We have tried to channel the activities of these kids, but we have not done it quite correctly. I do not think we

February 28, 1974
The Address-Mr. Danson
should be ashamed, not at all. I think we have tried very hard. However, when we do these things I think we must use some sort of structure and guidance. Speaking as a father, of course, I have seen the necessity for this. Your little boys grow up and you think they are adults and know what they are doing, but there are times when you realize that they are not. Then you realize that all of us need both someone to talk to and guidance based on experience. That is why during the recess I talked about a national youth service, a voluntary service which might use, perhaps, the infrastructure of the armed services for organization, transportation and accommodation. I raised this matter because it has concerned me for some time. I am sure members have heard me speak about this before. The response to the idea was almost incredible.
People across the country heard me with interest. I have done surveys, both in my constituency and across the country, which show a very high rate of receptiveness to the idea. One survey I did involved the subject of compulsory service. I compiled some figures which I have before me tonight and to which I will refer in order to give some rough totals. Approximately 71 per cent of the people were in favour of a compulsory service. If you want to extrapolate and include those who had some reservations about a compulsory service, the figure for those in favour would be between 80 and 90 per cent of those surveyed. Of those in grades 1 to 8 who were surveyed, 76.9 per cent were in favour of a compulsory service. I am talking about a service you enter voluntarily. Of those who were in grades 9 to 13, 75.1 per cent were in favour. Of those who had technical college education, 78.4 were in favour. Of those with university education who were surveyed, 62.8 were in favour. If we look at the rest of the country we will find that the figures are amazingly consistent. The degree of receptiveness is a little higher in Quebec than the rest of the country. Generally, this idea was very well received.
Such a service would harness the energy of our youth, the enthusiasm of our youth and their desire to be of service to their country, and they would be doing something which would be extremely worth while. I like the voluntary aspect of the service, because I think it is very important for people to want to be in it. I would put a hooker in that relating to unemployment insurance, which I shall deal with if I have time. Fundamentally, the program should be voluntary. If you make the program totally compulsory you would need to bring to it all the apparatus of military discipline. I do not think that is so bad. I had five years of it and survived-some of it behind bars, true, but I survived. However, that sort of program is not really what we are looking for in this country today.
If the program is voluntary, if it is well accepted and well motivated, the greatest punishment would be if you were kicked out of the service. Because the service would be voluntary, people would want to perform well. The kids involved in the program could move to other parts of the country and mix with other socio-economic groups. There could be a great Anglophone and Francophone interchange. They could meet other elements in society which sometimes we do not meet.
Think of the jobs these kids could do. I have listed them. They could include the development and maintenance of national, provincial and municipal parks and recreation

areas; work with handicapped, aged and native peoples. On second thoughts I would not include the native peoples generally as I think native people should work for native peoples. They could work with peoples of other disadvantaged groups. They could be involved in environmental clean-ups, and food and erosion control. They could work on forest fire prevention and on cleaning up, and could build fire breaks and access roads. They could be involved in agriculture, particularly in harvesting. They could work in the development and staffing of youth hostels. I just do not see why these things cannot be done. One could go on and on with such a list.
The commitment should be a serious one, say for one year's service. If you do well, perhaps you could be allowed to stay another year. Maybe the service could develop an administration, infrastructure and leadership of its own. The armed forces could give assistance in transportation, accommodation, administration and that sort of thing. Then, if you are really good and you want to stick at it, you might be allowed to stay a third year and maybe serve overseas.
That is the sort of program which I think could give purpose to our youth and give guidance and some sort of structure to those who want it and need it. A program like this would make kids feel that they are paying their dues to the society which has reared and educated them. There could be educational benefits when they have finished. For instance, those benefits could involve an equivalent period, say, or even double that period, at some educational institution. The possibilities are limitless. The need is there. There is a gap in our society which we are just beginning to identify. We have been searching and trying to find solutions. I do not say there is an easy answer. I think if we are genuine, people will respond genuinely, as they have responded to the participatory programs we have had.
I admit that these programs did not all work out well. Some of them worked very well, some of them worked out badly and some were disastrous. The mistakes we made were not for lack of trying. I would rather see us making mistakes by trying to do something than not doing anything at all.
I suggest that this idea should be considered seriously. It requires a pilot program. It should not be a Mickey Mouse program. The concept should be on a scale sufficiently large to get the program going. Then it can grow and we can build on it. We should only build with people who want to be in the program. It will be slow going at first, and because of that more people will want to be in it. It will be something like the summer employment program which really involves cadet training for the Armed Forces.
I think the kids will want to take part in the program. I suggest we can do as much with the kids who would take part in this program as we have done with kids who have taken part in the cadet training program. The program or service would be useful for kids who have left high school and have not yet taken up their university or business life. They need a break, they need to become mature and to be exposed to other people in society. Perhaps they need to

get their hands dirty and to have their backs aching. They will not mind that. I am sure they will want the challenge. We have not been providing it for them. Mr. Speaker, I urge that my suggestions receive the most serious consideration by all members in the House. I see that it is ten o'clock.
